images.caption:
The fortress of Humaitá in the wetlands of southern Paraguay.
The fortress was on a tight bend on the river Paraguay.  At the bottom of the map the river debouches into the river Paraná, the boundary with Argentina.  Notice the 3 km scale.  Base map in Schneider (1872: Berlin), "Der Krieg der Triple-Allianz", volume I.

images.caption: A detail from the Argentine painter's oil on canvas depicting the Paraguayan trench at the Battle of Curupayty (22 September 1866).  Pouring out a hail of grape and canister shot from a hastily erected earthwork, the Paraguayans inflicted the worst defeat the Allies (Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay) ever sustained.

images.caption: This map, which is an annotated version of the public domain map 'Atlas Historico da Guerra do Paraguay", Plates 4 and 5, by E.C. On the left is the River Paraguay; the fortress blocks its navigation.

images.caption: A band of Italian revolutionaries fighting in the Argentine army during the Paraguayan War.  These men, comrades of Garibaldi, fled Italy to South America and after many adventures are photographed at Tuyu-Cué in the wetlands of southern Paraguay.  Their colonel is Pipo Giribone (seated, right foreground).  This photograph must have been taken before early 1868, when Giribone was killed in a Paraguayan ambush.  The musicians (white headger) may have doubled as fighting men and certainly had the task of removing the wounded from battlefields.
images.alt: A band of Italian revolutionaries fighting in the Argentine army during the Paraguayan War.  These men, comrades of Garibaldi, fled Italy to South America and after many adventures are photographed at Tuyu-Cué in the wetlands of southern Paraguay.  Their colonel is Pipo Giribone (seated, right foreground).  This photograph must have been taken before early 1868, when Giribone was killed in a Paraguayan ambush.  The musicians (white headger) may have doubled as fighting men and certainly had the task of removing the wounded from battlefields.

images.caption: In the Paraguayan War, the outwork or redoubt called "Estabelecimento Novo" by the Brazilians ("Cierva" by the Paraguayans).  This map shows that the outwork was not on the River Paraguay, as the Allies had thought, but on the shore of an inland lagoon.  It had no strategic value; it was a bluff.  Its hard-fought capture on 19 February 1868 with serious loss of life turned out to be pointless.  (Base map by E.C. Jourdan of the Brazilian engineering corps, about 1870.)

images.caption:
An earthwork profile as used by the Paraguayan forces at the fortress of Humaitá.  Artillery on wooden platforms (not shown) fired grape or canister i.e. towards the right.   The surface was usually revetted with turf sods.
This is a a cropped and annotated version of Plate V of George Thompson's "The War in Paraguay" (1869).
